title: In the North Atlantic, a tracer-calibrated winter-surface ventilation model gives the sign of sigma0 26.5 AOU changes and the 2012-2021 rise, but not the size of 1997-2012 changes (1988-2025)
abstract: Question: does the near-outcrop ventilation model that gave North Pacific sigma0 26.5 AOU gains of observed size (sci:4525c37f) also explain the North Atlantic (NA) AOU changes quantitatively? Approach: the same 2-D advection-diffusion model on the 26.5 surface (WOA23 geostrophic flow; ventilation rate lam0 exp(-gap/delta) from the gap between the late-winter surface density and 26.5), calibrated only on CFC-12/SF6 transit-time ages of A05, A16N, A20 and A22, forced with the WOA23 decadal late-winter surface maps (1955-2022), and compared with GLODAP line-pair AOU changes and the BATS series under a pre-registered plan. Results: the model fits the NA ages (best score 0.25; NP 0.40), and both basins choose the same parameter families. It gives the sign of 10 of 11 line-pair changes (r = 0.71) and the 2012-2021 AOU rise on A20/A22 in part (4.7-6.6 of 15.6-18.0 umol/kg in the best set), but the 1997-2003 rise and 2003-2012 fall are 5-20 times too small (slope 3.4; size test failed). At BATS the 3-yr series correlates (r = 0.80, p = 0.02) and the 1989-1998 to 2016-2025 change is 0.64 of the observed +12.0. In 196 random orders of the decade maps both correlations were as high in 1.5%. NP-calibrated parameter sets give 9-10 correct signs. The signal comes from the winter surface south of 45 N and west of 45 W; the decadal flow change alone gives the wrong sign. Before 1988 the model over-predicts the lower AOU at Bermuda (observed -1.8 and -3.5 against model -5 to -12 and -3.5 to -7.5 umol/kg). Limitations: decade-mean forcing cannot give single-winter events; few independent line pairs; the response size differs about 5-fold among equally good parameter sets; the depth change of 26.5 predicts the pair changes equally well (r = 0.75).
